Hon'ble Alok Mahra, J.
Mr. Bilal Ahmed, learned counsel for
the applicants.
2. Mr. Pramod Tiwari, learned A.G.A.
for the State.
3. Mr. Ashok Kumar Beniwal, learned
counsel for respondent nos.2 to 4 through
Video Conferencing.
4. Present application has been filed
seeking quashing of the charge-sheet as
well as the cognizance/summoning order
dated 10.04.2026 as well as entire
proceedings of Criminal Case No.356 of
2026 under Section 115(2), 190, 191(3),
351(2), 352 of B.N.S. pending in the court
of learned Civil Judge/Judicial Magistrate,
Roorkee, Haridwar along with the entire
criminal proceedings arising therefrom.
5. Learned counsel for the applicants
would submit that the complainant lodged
an F.I.R. alleging that the applicants had
attacked the complainant and his family
members and brutally assaulted the
complainant with lathis and dandas. It is
further alleged that the complainant and
his family members somehow managed to
save themselves from the alleged assault
and thereafter lodged the F.I.R. against

UKHC010182082026
2026:UHC:9337
the applicants. Upon completion of the
investigation, the investigating agency
submitted a charge-sheet against the
applicants, on the basis of which the
learned trial court took cognizance of the
offences and proceeded with the matter in
accordance with law.
6. Learned counsel for the applicant
would further submit that now the
applicants and respondents amicably
settled their dispute and do not wish to
pursue the criminal proceedings any
further. In this regard, a joint
compounding application (I.A. No.1 of
2026) duly supported by the affidavits of
the applicant as well as respondents has
been filed before this Court stating that
the matter has been resolved amicably
and that the complainant does not intend
to prosecute the applicant any further.
7. The applicants as well as the
respondents are present in person before
this Court and have been duly identified
by their respective learned counsel. Upon
interaction with the Court, the
respondents, who are the victims/injured
persons, have categorically stated that
they are neighbours of the applicants; that
they have not sustained any serious
injuries; that the dispute between the
parties has been amicably settled; and
that they do not wish to pursue the
criminal proceedings against the
applicants.
8. Learned State Counsel opposes the
application on the ground that the
allegations pertain to serious offences
alleged in the F.I.R., However, he does not
dispute the factum of compromise
between the parties nor the filing of the
joint compounding application supported
by their affidavits.

UKHC010182082026
2026:UHC:9337
9. Heard learned counsel for the parties
and perused the material available on
record.
10. From the material placed on record,
it appears that the dispute between the
parties arose out of a personal dispute
between the applicant and respondent no.
3. The presence of the complainant and
the injured/victims before this Court,
coupled with their categorical statements,
establishes that the compromise arrived at
between the parties is voluntary and
genuine and has been entered into
without any coercion, undue influence or
pressure. Although the offences alleged
against the applicants are non-compoundable, it is well settled that the
High Court, in exercise of its inherent
jurisdiction under Section 528 the BNSS,
may quash criminal proceedings in
respect of non-compoundable offences
where the dispute is predominantly
private or personal in nature and the
Court is satisfied that quashing the
proceedings would secure the ends of
justice and prevent abuse of the process of
law.
11. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Gian
Singh v. State of Punjab, (2012) 10 SCC
303, has held that the High Court may
exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash
criminal proceedings where the dispute is
predominantly private or personal in
nature and the parties have amicably
resolved their differences, provided that
such exercise of power is warranted in the
interests of justice. However, the nature
and gravity of the offence must be duly
considered.
12. Similarly, in Narinder Singh v. State
of Punjab, (2014) 6 SCC 466, the Hon'ble
Supreme Court laid down the principles
governing the exercise of inherent

UKHC010182082026
2026:UHC:9337
jurisdiction for quashing criminal
proceedings on the basis of a compromise.
The Court is required to consider, inter
alia, the nature and gravity of the offence,
the circumstances in which it was
committed and whether the continuation
of the criminal proceedings would serve
any useful purpose.
13. Further, in Parbatbhai Aahir v. State
of Gujarat, (2017) 9 SCC 641, the Hon'ble
Supreme Court reiterated that the
inherent power of the High Court is
intended to prevent abuse of the process
of the Court and to secure the ends of
justice, and that the decision to quash
criminal proceedings on the basis of a
settlement must be guided by the nature
of the offence and the facts and
circumstances of the particular case.
14. In the present case, the material on
record indicates that the parties are
neighbours and that the dispute arose out
of a personal altercation. The complainant
and the injured/victims, who are present
before this Court, have categorically stated
that the matter has been amicably settled
and that they do not wish to pursue the
criminal proceedings against the
applicants. Their statements do not
indicate any coercion or undue influence,
and the compromise appears to be
voluntary and genuine.
15. In view of the amicable settlement
between the parties and the categorical
statements made by the complainant and
the injured/victims, this Court is of the
considered opinion that, having regard to
the nature and circumstances of the
dispute, continuation of the criminal
proceedings would serve no useful
purpose and would not advance the ends
of justice. Accordingly, the present case
warrants consideration for exercise of the

UKHC010182082026
2026:UHC:9337
inherent jurisdiction of this Court under
Section 528 of the BNSS, subject to the
nature and gravity of the offences alleged.
16. Considering the totality of the facts
and circumstances of the case and the law
laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court
in the aforesaid judgments, this Court is
of the view that this is a fit case for
exercising the inherent powers to secure
the ends of justice and to prevent abuse of
the process of the Court.
17. Accordingly, the compounding
application (I.A. No.1 of 2026) is allowed.
18. Consequently, the charge-sheet as
well as the cognizance/summoning order
dated 10.04.2026 as well as entire
proceedings of Criminal Case No.356 of
2026 pending in the court of learned Civil
Judge/Judicial Magistrate, Roorkee,
Haridwar along with the entire criminal
proceedings arising therefrom are hereby
quashed.
19. The present C-528 application is,
accordingly, allowed.
20. Pending applications, if any, shall
stand disposed of.
 (Alok Mahra J.) 13.10.2026 Mamta
